Question:
A game board consists of \(64\) squares that alternate between shaded and unshaded. The figure below shows square \(P\) in the bottom row and square \(Q\) in the top row. A marker is placed at \(P.\) A step consists of moving the marker onto one of the adjoining unshaded squares in the row above. How many \(7\)-step paths are there from \(P\) to \(Q?\) (The figure shows a sample path.)

[Figure 1](figures/2020_AMC_8_Q21_question_fig1.svg)
Solution:
Build the path count one row at a time. Any path reaching a square must come from one of the two diagonally adjacent squares just below it. Therefore its count is the sum of those two earlier counts; a square outside the board contributes nothing.

Start with one path at \(P\). The two reachable squares in the next row each get \(1\). In the following row, the middle reachable square gets \(1+1=2\), while each outside reachable square gets \(1\).

Continue this addition rule upward. The diagram shows counts only for squares that can still lead to \(Q\). Some blank squares can be reached from \(P\), but cannot reach \(Q\) in the remaining steps. A blank here therefore does not necessarily mean zero paths:

[Figure 2](figures/2020_AMC_8_Q21_solution_official_paths.png)

For example, the square labeled \(10\) receives \(4+6\) paths. At the top, \(Q\) receives \(19+9=\boxed{28}\) paths, choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

Every path has exactly one last step, so adding predecessor counts includes each path once. Working inside the board also excludes paths that would cross its edge.
